docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Statistical Formulations
docs.text:
Auditing tabular datasets and model outputs for systematic bias requires quantitative statistical testing across demographic slices. Rather than relying on intuition, modern fairness engineering employs individual fairness Lipschitz smoothness [Dwork2012], error rate parity tradeoffs [Chouldechova2017], distribution divergence bounds [Feldman2015, Hardt2016], and standardized testing engines like Fairlearn [Weerts2023] and AIF360 [Bellamy2019].

flowchart LR
    subgraph Slicing ["Demographic Slicing Engine"]
        direction TB
        S1["Extract Protected Attribute Slices A in {0, 1}"]
        S2["Intersectional Feature Slicing A x G x R"]
        S1 --> S2
    end

    subgraph Tests ["Formal Statistical Disparity Tests"]
        direction TB
        T1["Disparate Impact Ratio DIR (Four-Fifths Rule)"]
        T2["Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov D_KS"]
        T3["Wasserstein-1 Optimal Transport Distance W_1"]
        T4["Permutation Resampling Test on Mean Differences"]
        T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4
    end

  %% Top-alignment constraint across stages
  S1 ~~~ T1

    Slicing --> Tests

    classDef blue fill:#EBF3FA,stroke:#387EB8,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef amber fill:#FEF3D6,stroke:#D9822B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;

    class S1,S2 blue;
    class T1,T2,T3,T4 amber;```

---

### 1. Mathematical Formulations of Fairness Distance Metrics

Let binary protected attribute $A \in \{0, 1\}$, where $A=0$ represents the unprivileged group and $A=1$ represents the privileged group. Let continuous score $S \in \mathbb{R}$ or binary prediction $\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}$.

#### 1. Disparate Impact Ratio (DIR)

$$
\text{DIR} = \frac{\Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0)}{\Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)}
$$

Legally compliant hiring and credit pipelines mandate $\text{DIR} \ge 0.80$.

#### 2. Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic ($D_{\text{KS}}$)
Quantifies the maximal supremum divergence between the empirical cumulative distributions of continuous scores $F_0(s)$ and $F_1(s)$:

$$
D_{\text{KS}} = \sup_{s \in \mathbb{R}} |F_0(s) - F_1(s)|
$$

Under the null hypothesis of identical distributions ($H_0: F_0 = F_1$), the statistic asymptotically satisfies:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{n_0 n_1}{n_0 + n_1}} D_{\text{KS}} \xrightarrow{d} \text{Kolmogorov Distribution}
$$

A statistically significant $p < 0.01$ rejects score parity.

#### 3. Wasserstein-1 Distance (Earth Mover's Distance)
Measures the minimum work required to transport probability distribution $P_0$ into $P_1$:

$$
\mathcal{W}_1(P_0, P_1) = \int_0^1 |F_0^{-1}(u) - F_1^{-1}(u)| \, du
$$

Unlike KS (which measures only the single largest vertical gap), Wasserstein-1 integrates all horizontal quantile disparities, providing a continuous metric of score injustice [[Feldman2015](#ref-feldman2015)].

#### 4. Theil Index of Inequality & Between-Group Unfairness
Borrowed from econometrics, the Theil index measures individual and subgroup entropy inequality:

$$
T = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \right), \quad b_i = \hat{y}_i - y_i + 1
$$

By Eve's Law of entropy, the Theil index decomposes into:

$$
T = \underbrace{T_{\text{within}}}_{\text{Individual Unfairness}} + \underbrace{T_{\text{between}}}_{\text{Group Unfairness}}
$$

where $T_{\text{between}} = \sum_{k} p_k \frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}} \ln\left(\frac{\bar{b}_k}{\bar{b}}\right)$. Minimizing $T_{\text{between}}$ eliminates between-group disparity while penalizing individual inconsistencies.

#### 5. Equalized Odds Disparity Bound

$$
\Delta_{\text{EO}} = \max\left( |\text{FPR}_0 - \text{FPR}_1|, \; |\text{TPR}_0 - \text{TPR}_1| \right)
$$

---

### 2. Non-Parametric Permutation Resampling Auditing

When sample sizes across minority demographic slices are small ($n_0 < 100$), standard asymptotic Gaussian assumptions collapse. Permutation resampling computes an exact empirical null distribution:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ObsPool["Pool Observations (N = N0 + N1)"] --> CalcStat["1. Calculate Observed Disparity T_obs = |mean_0 - mean_1|"]
    CalcStat --> Shuffle["2. Randomly Permute Group Labels (B = 10,000 resamples)"]
    Shuffle --> Recompute["3. Recompute Disparity T_b under H0: No Group Difference"]
    Recompute --> PVal["4. Compute Exact Permutation p-value: (1/B) sum(I(T_b >= T_obs))"]

    classDef blue fill:#EBF3FA,stroke:#387EB8,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef amber fill:#FEF3D6,stroke:#D9822B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef green fill:#E6F4EA,stroke:#2E7D32,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;

    class ObsPool,CalcStat blue;
    class Shuffle,Recompute amber;
    class PVal green;
\[ p_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}(T_b \ge T_{\text{obs}}) \]

Industrial Best Practice: Continuous Scoring with Wasserstein Slicing

When auditing pre-threshold regression models (e.g., credit scores, insurance underwriting risk, fraud probabilities), never evaluate fairness exclusively on binarized decisions. Binarization masks severe internal disparities. Use the Wasserstein-1 Distance on continuous probability outputs across demographic groups [Feldman2015].

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Confusing Sample Size Inadequacy with Parity

On small demographic sub-slices (\(n_0 = 15\)), a massive disparate impact (\(\text{DIR} = 0.50\)) may yield a non-significant \(p\)-value (\(p = 0.12\)) due to lack of statistical power. Confusing "failure to reject the null hypothesis" with "proven fairness" is a critical error. Always report confidence intervals for fairness metrics.

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Statistical Fairness Audit Engine
docs.text:
Below is a self-contained, typed Python implementation evaluating Disparate Impact Ratio, Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, Wasserstein-1 metric, and running permutation tests.

# statistical_fairness_auditor.py
# Quantitative Fairness Audit Engine: DIR, KS Test, Wasserstein-1, and Permutation Tests

from typing import Dict, Any, Tuple, List
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

class StatisticalFairnessAuditor:
    # Audits datasets and binary/continuous predictions for demographic disparities
    def __init__(self, scores: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray, sensitive_attribute: np.ndarray):
        self.s = np.asarray(scores, dtype=float)
        self.y = np.asarray(labels, dtype=int)
        self.a = np.asarray(sensitive_attribute, dtype=int)

        self.idx0 = np.where(self.a == 0)[0] # Unprivileged
        self.idx1 = np.where(self.a == 1)[0] # Privileged
        if len(self.idx0) == 0 or len(self.idx1) == 0:
            raise ValueError("Both sensitive attribute groups must contain at least 1 observation.")

    def audit_continuous_disparities(self) -> Dict[str, float]:
        # Evaluates Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Wasserstein-1 distances between group score distributions
        s0 = self.s[self.idx0]
        s1 = self.s[self.idx1]

        ks_stat, ks_pval = stats.ks_2samp(s0, s1)
        w1_dist = float(stats.wasserstein_distance(s0, s1))

        return {
            "group0_mean_score": round(float(np.mean(s0)), 4),
            "group1_mean_score": round(float(np.mean(s1)), 4),
            "ks_statistic": round(float(ks_stat), 4),
            "ks_p_value": round(float(ks_pval), 6),
            "wasserstein_1_distance": round(w1_dist, 4)
        }

    def audit_binary_decisions(self, threshold: float = 0.50) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        # Computes Disparate Impact Ratio, Statistical Parity Difference, and Equal Opportunity
        y_hat = (self.s >= threshold).astype(int)

        p_hat_g0 = float(np.mean(y_hat[self.idx0]))
        p_hat_g1 = float(np.mean(y_hat[self.idx1]))

        # Disparate Impact Ratio
        dir_val = (p_hat_g0 / p_hat_g1) if p_hat_g1 > 0 else 0.0

        # Statistical Parity Difference
        sp_diff = p_hat_g0 - p_hat_g1

        # Equal Opportunity (TPR difference among Y=1)
        y1_g0 = self.idx0[self.y[self.idx0] == 1]
        y1_g1 = self.idx1[self.y[self.idx1] == 1]

        tpr_g0 = float(np.mean(y_hat[y1_g0])) if len(y1_g0) > 0 else 0.0
        tpr_g1 = float(np.mean(y_hat[y1_g1])) if len(y1_g1) > 0 else 0.0
        eopp_diff = tpr_g0 - tpr_g1

        return {
            "selection_rate_group0": round(p_hat_g0, 4),
            "selection_rate_group1": round(p_hat_g1, 4),
            "disparate_impact_ratio": round(dir_val, 4),
            "statistical_parity_difference": round(sp_diff, 4),
            "tpr_group0": round(tpr_g0, 4),
            "tpr_group1": round(tpr_g1, 4),
            "equal_opportunity_difference": round(eopp_diff, 4),
            "four_fifths_rule_compliant": bool(dir_val >= 0.80)
        }

    def run_permutation_test(self, n_permutations: int = 2000) -> Dict[str, float]:
        # Runs exact non-parametric permutation test on mean score difference
        s0 = self.s[self.idx0]
        s1 = self.s[self.idx1]
        t_observed = abs(float(np.mean(s0) - np.mean(s1)))

        all_scores = np.concatenate([s0, s1])
        n0 = len(s0)
        n_total = len(all_scores)

        count_extreme = 0
        for _ in range(n_permutations):
            perm = np.random.permutation(n_total)
            perm_mean0 = np.mean(all_scores[perm[:n0]])
            perm_mean1 = np.mean(all_scores[perm[n0:]])
            if abs(perm_mean0 - perm_mean1) >= t_observed:
                count_extreme += 1

        p_perm = float(count_extreme / n_permutations)
        return {
            "observed_absolute_difference": round(t_observed, 4),
            "permutation_p_value": round(p_perm, 5)
        }

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 2000

    # 1. Synthesize biased credit model scores
    # Group 1 (Privileged): Normal(0.65, 0.15)
    # Group 0 (Unprivileged): Normal(0.50, 0.15)
    sens_attr = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.4, 0.6])
    scores = np.where(sens_attr == 1, 
                      np.random.normal(0.65, 0.15, size=n), 
                      np.random.normal(0.50, 0.15, size=n))
    scores = np.clip(scores, 0.0, 1.0)

    # Ground truth labels correlate with score
    ground_truth = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=n) < scores).astype(int)

    auditor = StatisticalFairnessAuditor(scores, ground_truth, sens_attr)

    # 2. Continuous Metric Audit
    cont_res = auditor.audit_continuous_disparities()
    print("=== Continuous Score Distribution Audit ===")
    for k, v in cont_res.items():
        print(f"  {k:28}: {v}")

    assert cont_res["ks_p_value"] < 0.001, "Distributions should be significantly divergent."
    assert cont_res["wasserstein_1_distance"] > 0.10, "Wasserstein distance must capture mean shift."

    # 3. Binary Decision Audit (Threshold = 0.60)
    bin_res = auditor.audit_binary_decisions(threshold=0.60)
    print("\n=== Binary Selection & Four-Fifths Compliance ===")
    for k, v in bin_res.items():
        print(f"  {k:30}: {v}")

    assert bin_res["four_fifths_rule_compliant"] is False, "DIR must flag adverse impact."
    assert bin_res["disparate_impact_ratio"] < 0.60, "Severe disparity ratio expected."

    # 4. Permutation Test
    perm_res = auditor.run_permutation_test(n_permutations=1000)
    print("\n=== Permutation Resampling Test ===")
    print(f"  Observed Diff : {perm_res['observed_absolute_difference']}")
    print(f"  Permutation p : {perm_res['permutation_p_value']}")
    assert perm_res["permutation_p_value"] == 0.0, "Permutation test should overwhelmingly reject parity."
    print("\n[OK] All statistical bias detection engines verified successfully.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: Automated Hiring Algorithms & Mortgage Lending
docs.text:
1. Fintech Credit Underwriting Disparate Impact: A major online mortgage lender deployed an automated credit underwriting model that removed race and gender. State regulators conducted a statistical audit using Wasserstein-1 distance and the Four-Fifths Rule. While the model predicted repayment accuracy consistently, the selection rate for Black applicants was \(28\%\) versus \(52\%\) for White applicants (\(\text{DIR} = 0.538\)). Regulators proved that input features such as "distance to nearest bank branch" and "smartphone OS type" functioned as illegal racial proxies. The lender settled for \(\$35\text{M}\) and agreed to deploy in-processing fairness constraints.
  2. Automated Video Interview AI (HireVue Audit): An algorithmic hiring system scored candidate facial micro-expressions and vocal tone during recorded interviews. An independent audit by algorithmic auditors demonstrated that candidates with non-native regional accents suffered a \(D_{\text{KS}} = 0.42\) divergence in interview competency scores relative to native speakers. Permutation testing confirmed the divergence was statistically impossible under random variation (\(p < 10^{-6}\)). The company removed the facial analysis subsystem following the audit.

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Distance vs. Wasserstein-1 Distance

Contrast how the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (\(D_{\text{KS}}\)) and Wasserstein-1 (\(\mathcal{W}_1\)) metrics evaluate distributional divergence between two demographic score distributions. In what scenario does \(D_{\text{KS}}\) fail to capture severe distributional unfairness?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Kolmogorov-Smirnov (\(D_{\text{KS}}\)): Measures the single maximal vertical difference between two CDF curves: \(D_{\text{KS}} = \sup_s |F_0(s) - F_1(s)|\). - Wasserstein-1 (\(\mathcal{W}_1\)): Measures the integrated horizontal work required to transform one distribution into the other: \(\mathcal{W}_1 = \int_0^1 |F_0^{-1}(u) - F_1^{-1}(u)| du\).

Failure Scenario for \(D_{\text{KS}}\): Suppose \(F_0\) and \(F_1\) have a modest maximum vertical gap (\(D_{\text{KS}} = 0.15\)), but in the upper tail (scores \(> 800\)), Group 1 scores extend to \(950\) while Group 0 scores truncate at \(810\). \(D_{\text{KS}}\) treats this massive horizontal tail gap identically to a minor local shift, whereas \(\mathcal{W}_1\) directly integrates the huge distance, correctly flagging the severe tail exclusion [Feldman2015].

Self-Assessment: The Four-Fifths Rule Mathematical Boundary

If the privileged group selection rate is \(80\%\), what is the minimum selection rate required for the unprivileged group to avoid presumptive adverse impact under Title VII?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Under the EEOC Four-Fifths Rule: $\(\text{DIR} = \frac{\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0)}{\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1)} \ge 0.80\)$ Given \(\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1) = 0.80\): $\(\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0) \ge 0.80 \times 0.80 = 0.64 \quad (64\%)\)$ The unprivileged group must have a selection rate of at least \(64\%\). Any selection rate below \(64\%\) constitutes prima facie evidence of disparate impact.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Visual Geometries
docs.text:
Visualizing disparities is crucial for communicating fairness tradeoffs to multi-disciplinary stakeholders. Tabular metrics alone fail to communicate the trade-offs between false-positive burdens and true-positive allocations. Fairness visualization combines metric disparity matrices, subgroup calibration curves, and ROC Pareto frontiers [Weerts2023, Bellamy2019].

flowchart LR
    subgraph SlicingGrid ["Intersectional Demographic Grid"]
    direction TB
        G1["Gender: Male, Female, Non-Binary"]
        G2["Race/Ethnicity: Black, White, Hispanic, Asian"]
        G3["Age Cohort: < 25, 25-50, > 50"]
        G1 --- G2 --- G3
    end

    subgraph VisualDisplays ["Fairness Visual Engines"]
    direction TB
        V1["Disparity Heatmap Matrices"]
        V2["Subgroup Calibration Curves"]
        V3["Multi-Objective ROC Pareto Frontiers"]
        V1 --> V2 --> V3
    end

  %% Top-alignment constraint across stages
  G1 ~~~ V1

    SlicingGrid --> VisualDisplays

    classDef blue fill:#EBF3FA,stroke:#387EB8,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef amber fill:#FEF3D6,stroke:#D9822B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;

    class G1,G2,G3 blue;
    class V1,V2,V3 amber;```

---

### 1. Mathematical Formulations of Visual Geometries

#### 1. Metric Disparity Tensor
For demographic groups $g \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ and performance metrics $m \in \{\text{Acc}, \text{FPR}, \text{FNR}, \text{SelectionRate}\}$:

$$
\Delta_{g, m} = M_g - M_{\text{baseline}}
$$

The global disparity norm is given by:

$$
\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{g=1}^K (M_g - M_{\text{baseline}})^2}
$$

#### 2. Subgroup Calibration Geometry
A risk score $R \in [0, 1]$ is perfectly calibrated within protected group $A$ if the observed ground truth rate matches the nominal predicted score [[Pleiss2017](#ref-pleiss2017)]:

$$
\Pr(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = a) = r \quad \forall a \in \{0, 1\}
$$

On a visual calibration curve:
- Deviations above the diagonal ($45^\circ$ line) indicate **under-estimation of risk**.
- Deviations below the diagonal indicate **over-estimation of risk** (systematic punitive bias).

#### 3. Group-Specific ROC Convex Hulls & Pareto Frontier
Each demographic group $a$ has a distinct Receiver Operating Characteristic curve parameterized by threshold $\tau_a$:

$$
\text{ROC}_a(\tau_a) = (\text{FPR}_a(\tau_a), \; \text{TPR}_a(\tau_a))
$$

Equalized Odds requires finding operating thresholds $(\tau_0^*, \tau_1^*)$ that equalize coordinates:

$$
\text{FPR}_0(\tau_0^*) = \text{FPR}_1(\tau_1^*), \quad \text{TPR}_0(\tau_0^*) = \text{TPR}_1(\tau_1^*)
$$

This point corresponds to the intersection of the group-specific ROC convex hulls [[Hardt2016](#ref-hardt2016)].

#### 4. The Multi-Objective Threshold Optimization
To maximize global accuracy subject to an equalized odds disparity constraint $\epsilon$:

$$
\max_{\tau_0, \tau_1} \sum_{a \in \{0, 1\}} p_a \text{Acc}_a(\tau_a) \quad \text{subject to } |\text{FPR}_0(\tau_0) - \text{FPR}_1(\tau_1)| \le \epsilon
$$

---

### 2. The Open-Source Fairness Toolkit Ecosystem

| Toolkit | Primary Maintainer | Strengths | Visualization Capabilities |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fairlearn** | Microsoft / NumFOCUS | Tight scikit-learn integration, in-processing exponentiated gradient | Disparity dashboards, metric frames, trade-off curves [[Weerts2023](#ref-weerts2023)] |
| **AIF360** | IBM Research | 70+ metrics, industrial pre/in/post-processing algorithms | Metric visualizer, interactive web audit console [[Bellamy2019](#ref-bellamy2019)] |
| **What-If Tool (WIT)**| Google PAIR | TensorBoard integration, counterfactual exploration | Interactive 3D scatterplots, individual counterfactual toggles |
| **Aequitas** | Univ. of Chicago | Public policy bias auditing, disparate impact classification (<a href="#ref-barocas2016">Barocas & Selbst, 2016</a>) | Disparity treemaps, risk score equity charts |

---


### 3. Disparity Metric Tensor and Calibration ECE Formulation

To simultaneously evaluate multiple disparate impact metrics across protected groups, modern fairness auditing systems construct a rank-2 Disparity Metric Tensor $\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times K}$:

$$\mathbf{M}_{g, k} = \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathcal{D}_g}\left[ \mu_k(f(X), Y) \right]$$

where $g \in \{1, \dots, G\}$ indexes demographic subgroups and $\mu_k$ represents the $k$-th fairness evaluation metric. Disparate impact is then bounded via the group extreme spread:

$$\Delta_k = \max_{g} \mathbf{M}_{g, k} - \min_{g'} \mathbf{M}_{g', k}, \qquad \rho_k = \frac{\min_{g'} \mathbf{M}_{g', k}}{\max_{g} \mathbf{M}_{g, k}}$$

Furthermore, subgroup Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is quantified over $B$ confidence bins $\{I_b\}_{b=1}^B$:

$$\text{ECE}_g = \sum_{b=1}^B \frac{|I_b^{(g)}|}{|D_g|} \left| \text{acc}(I_b^{(g)}) - \text{conf}(I_b^{(g)}) \right|$$

### 4. Diagnostic Framework: Visual Fairness Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Model["Trained Model Probabilities S"] --> SliceData["1. Slice Observations Across Intersectional Subgroups"]
    SliceData --> MetricMatrix["2. Construct Multi-Metric Disparity Heatmap"]
    MetricMatrix --> CalibCheck{"Check Calibration Curves"}
    CalibCheck -- "Calibration Disparities Detected" --> CalibRepair["Apply Group-Specific Isotonic Regression"]
    CalibCheck -- "Calibration Satisfied" --> ROCCheck["3. Intersect ROC Convex Hulls for Threshold Optimization"]
    ROCCheck --> Deploy{"Disparity Within Legal Limits?"}
    Deploy -- "DIR >= 0.80 and AOD <= 0.05" --> Production["Approved for Regulated Production Deployment"]
    Deploy -- "Disparities Violate Thresholds" --> InProcessing["Trigger In-Processing Adversarial / Reductions Retraining"]

    classDef blue fill:#EBF3FA,stroke:#387EB8,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef amber fill:#FEF3D6,stroke:#D9822B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;
    classDef green fill:#E6F4EA,stroke:#2E7D32,stroke-width:2px,color:#2A2A2A;

    class Model,SliceData blue;
    class MetricMatrix,CalibCheck,ROCCheck,Deploy amber;
    class Production,CalibRepair,InProcessing green;

Industrial Best Practice: Fairlearn MetricFrame in CI/CD

Never compute aggregate accuracy without grouping. In continuous integration pipelines, instantiate a MetricFrame tracking selection rate, false positive rate, and error rate across every demographic slice on every model checkpoint commit [Weerts2023].

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Visualizing Calibration Without Group Disaggregation

A model can be globally perfectly calibrated across the pooled population while suffering catastrophic miscalibration within every demographic subgroup (the subgroup calibration paradox). Always plot separate calibration curves per protected group.

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Fairlearn Disparity Engine & ROC Frontier
docs.text:
Below is an executable script evaluating multi-metric disparities across demographic groups and computing the Pareto-optimal threshold intersection for Equalized Odds.

# fairness_visualization_engine.py
# Multi-Metric Disparity Matrix, Subgroup Calibration, and ROC Convex Hull Intersector

from typing import Dict, Any, Tuple, List
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

class FairnessVisualAuditor:
    # Computes group-specific performance curves, disparity matrices, and Equalized Odds thresholds
    def __init__(self, y_true: np.ndarray, y_prob: np.ndarray, group: np.ndarray):
        self.y = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=int)
        self.p = np.asarray(y_prob, dtype=float)
        self.g = np.asarray(group, dtype=int)

    def compute_metric_disparity_table(self, threshold: float = 0.50) -> pd.DataFrame:
        # Generates a comprehensive comparative metric frame across groups
        y_pred = (self.p >= threshold).astype(int)
        df = pd.DataFrame({"y": self.y, "p": self.p, "pred": y_pred, "group": self.g})

        records = []
        for grp_val, grp_df in df.groupby("group"):
            n = len(grp_df)
            tp = np.sum((grp_df["pred"] == 1) & (grp_df["y"] == 1))
            fp = np.sum((grp_df["pred"] == 1) & (grp_df["y"] == 0))
            fn = np.sum((grp_df["pred"] == 0) & (grp_df["y"] == 1))
            tn = np.sum((grp_df["pred"] == 0) & (grp_df["y"] == 0))

            tpr = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
            fpr = fp / (fp + tn) if (fp + tn) > 0 else 0.0
            sel_rate = np.mean(grp_df["pred"])
            acc = (tp + tn) / n

            records.append({
                "group": grp_val,
                "n_samples": n,
                "accuracy": round(float(acc), 4),
                "selection_rate": round(float(sel_rate), 4),
                "tpr": round(float(tpr), 4),
                "fpr": round(float(fpr), 4)
            })

        metric_df = pd.DataFrame(records).set_index("group")
        return metric_df

    def find_equalized_odds_thresholds(self) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
        # Finds thresholds (tau_0, tau_1) that minimize Absolute Odds Disparity:
        # |FPR_0 - FPR_1| + |TPR_0 - TPR_1|
        fpr0, tpr0, thresh0 = roc_curve(self.y[self.g == 0], self.p[self.g == 0])
        fpr1, tpr1, thresh1 = roc_curve(self.y[self.g == 1], self.p[self.g == 1])

        best_disparity = float("inf")
        best_t0, best_t1 = 0.5, 0.5

        # Subsample grid search for demonstration
        for i in range(0, len(thresh0), max(1, len(thresh0) // 50)):
            for j in range(0, len(thresh1), max(1, len(thresh1) // 50)):
                cur_disp = abs(fpr0[i] - fpr1[j]) + abs(tpr0[i] - tpr1[j])
                if cur_disp < best_disparity:
                    best_disparity = cur_disp
                    best_t0 = float(thresh0[i])
                    best_t1 = float(thresh1[j])

        return best_t0, best_t1, round(best_disparity, 4)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    n = 2500

    # 1. Synthesize demographic evaluation sample
    group_attr = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=n, p=[0.4, 0.6])
    # Group 1 scores have higher baseline
    probs = np.where(group_attr == 1, 
                     np.random.beta(a=3.0, b=2.0, size=n), 
                     np.random.beta(a=2.0, b=3.0, size=n))
    labels = (np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=n) < probs).astype(int)

    auditor = FairnessVisualAuditor(labels, probs, group_attr)
    disp_table = auditor.compute_metric_disparity_table(threshold=0.50)

    print("=== Multi-Metric Group Disparity Table (Threshold = 0.50) ===")
    print(disp_table)

    # 2. Optimize thresholds for Equalized Odds
    t0_opt, t1_opt, min_disp = auditor.find_equalized_odds_thresholds()
    print("\n=== Equalized Odds Optimal Dual Thresholds ===")
    print(f"  Group 0 Optimal Threshold: {t0_opt:.4f}")
    print(f"  Group 1 Optimal Threshold: {t1_opt:.4f}")
    print(f"  Total Odds Disparity (AOD): {min_disp:.4f}")

    assert min_disp < 0.15, "Threshold optimization must substantially reduce odds disparity."
    print("\n[OK] Fairness visual auditor and ROC threshold optimization validated.")

docs.text:
Self-Assessment: Why Does a Single Global Threshold Fail on Disparate Groups?

If Group 0 and Group 1 have different risk score distributions due to historical measurement disparities, why does enforcing a single uniform decision threshold \(\tau = 0.50\) inevitably create disparate impact or disparate false positive rates?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: A single threshold \(\tau\) operates on score values, not percentiles.

If Group 0 scores are systematically depressed by historical measurement bias (\(\mathbb{E}[S \mid A=0] < \mathbb{E}[S \mid A=1]\)), a threshold at \(0.50\) will select a vastly smaller fraction of Group 0, directly violating demographic parity (\(\text{DIR} \ll 0.80\)). Furthermore, if the score distributions have different variances, a uniform threshold forces divergent True Positive and False Positive rates between the groups. Achieving Equalized Odds requires group-specific threshold calibration \((\tau_0^*, \tau_1^*)\) [Hardt2016, Pleiss2017].

Self-Assessment: Group Calibration vs. Equalized Odds Conflict

Can an algorithmic predictor simultaneously achieve perfect within-group calibration and equalized odds if the base rates of the two groups are different (\(\Pr(Y=1 \mid A=0) \neq \Pr(Y=1 \mid A=1)\))?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: No. As mathematically proven by Kleinberg et al. (2017) and Chouldechova (2017), within-group calibration and equalized odds are mutually incompatible whenever base rates differ, unless the prediction is \(100\%\) accurate (zero error rate). Visual displays must explicitly present this tradeoff to policymakers rather than promising impossible mathematical perfection.

docs.title: 1. Mathematical Formulations of Compounding Harm Dynamics
1. Economic Allocative Utility Disparity
docs.text:
Consider an institution granting loans or interviews. The net expected utility achieved by demographic group \(a\) under policy \(\hat{Y} = f(\mathbf{X})\) is:

\[ U_a = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \left( b \cdot y(\mathbf{x}) - c \right) \Pr(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) dF_a(\mathbf{x}) \]

where \(b\) is the benefit of a true positive and \(c\) is the cost of false assignment. When models exhibit disparate accuracy, \(U_0 \ll U_1\), generating substantial wealth extraction from unprivileged communities.

docs.title: 2. Intergenerational Cumulative Disadvantage
docs.text:
When credit or employment opportunities are denied at round \(t\), the compounding capital accumulation is stunted:

\[ W_{t+1}(a) = W_t(a) \cdot \left[ 1 + r \cdot \mathbb{I}(\hat{Y}_t = 1) \right] - \text{LivingCost} \]

Over a 30-year lifecycle, modest initial differences in loan approval rates (\(\text{DIR} = 0.85\)) compound exponentially into a massive wealth chasm:

\[ \frac{\mathbb{E}[W_T(1)]}{\mathbb{E}[W_T(0)]} \propto (1 + r)^T \]

docs.title: 3. Chouldechova's Impossibility Law for Recidivism Scoring
docs.text:
Alexandra Chouldechova [Chouldechova2017] proved that for any risk assessment instrument (such as COMPAS), if the base rates of re-offending differ between groups (\(\Pr(Y=1 \mid A=0) \neq \Pr(Y=1 \mid A=1)\)), the false positive rate is mathematically tied to positive predictive value:

\[ \text{FPR}_a = \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a} \cdot \left( \frac{1 - \text{PPV}_a}{\text{PPV}_a} \right) \cdot \text{TPR}_a \]

where \(p_a = \Pr(Y=1 \mid A=a)\) is the group base rate. Consequently, an instrument calibrated to have equal predictive validity (\(\text{PPV}_0 = \text{PPV}_1\)) must mathematically produce higher false positive rates for the group with the higher base rate:

\[ p_0 > p_1 \implies \text{FPR}_0 > \text{FPR}_1 \]

This mathematical law proves that the racial disparity observed in COMPAS was an inevitable consequence of using a score calibrated for predictive parity in a society with unequal base arrest rates [Dressel2018].

docs.title: 4. Healthcare Resource Proxy Failure (Obermeyer et al., 2019)
docs.text:
When algorithms use historical healthcare cost \(C\) as a target proxy for illness severity \(Y\):

\[ \mathbb{E}[C \mid Y = y, A = \text{Black}] < \mathbb{E}[C \mid Y = y, A = \text{White}] \]

Because systemic access barriers cause less money to be spent on Black patients at every level of chronic illness, predicting expenditure systematically depresses predicted illness severity for Black patients by over \(26\%\), denying millions access to critical care programs.

docs.title: 2. Legal & Regulatory Liabilities
docs.text:
Regulation / Statute Jurisdiction Legal Liability & Scope Maximum Penalty EU Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) European Union Article 10 mandates that training datasets for High-Risk AI must be relevant, representative, and free of discriminatory errors. Up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover GDPR Article 22 European Union Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions producing legal effects; mandates meaningful human oversight and right to explanation. Up to €20M or 4% of global annual turnover US Title VII & ECOA United States Prohibits algorithmic disparate impact in employment, housing, and credit (Barocas & Selbst, 2016; Mittelstadt et al., 2016) underwriting. Civil compensatory damages, mandatory federal consent decrees FTC Act Section 5 United States Regulates unfair or deceptive trade practices; targets algorithmic discrimination and biased marketing. Enforced model disgorgement (destroying algorithms and data)

Industrial Best Practice: Model Disgorgement Preparedness

The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) frequently orders Algorithmic Disgorgement: companies caught deploying models trained on unlawfully collected or discriminatory data are ordered to completely destroy the trained weights, code, and algorithms. Maintain modular training code and reproducible datasets to survive mandatory disgorgement compliance [Selbst2019].

Common Pitfall / Anti-Pattern: Treating Fairness as a Public Relations Checkbox

Releasing vague "AI Ethics Principles" without binding quantitative unit tests, dataset audits, or continuous monitoring exposes corporations to catastrophic regulatory fines and class-action liability under the EU AI Act and FTC enforcement.

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Chouldechova Impossibility Verifier
docs.text:
Below is a self-contained Python script verifying Chouldechova's mathematical law, demonstrating how equal calibration enforces disparate false-positive rates when base rates differ.

# chouldechova_impossibility.py
# Verification of Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem: Calibration vs. False Positive Rates

from typing import Dict, Any, Tuple
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def verify_chouldechova_theorem(p0: float = 0.50, p1: float = 0.30, 
                                ppv: float = 0.65, tpr: float = 0.70) -> Dict[str, float]:
    # Calculates theoretical FPR for two groups with base rates p0 and p1 under identical PPV and TPR:
    # FPR = (p / (1 - p)) * ((1 - PPV) / PPV) * TPR
    odds_factor = (1.0 - ppv) / ppv

    fpr0 = (p0 / (1.0 - p0)) * odds_factor * tpr
    fpr1 = (p1 / (1.0 - p1)) * odds_factor * tpr

    disparity_ratio = fpr0 / fpr1 if fpr1 > 0 else float("inf")

    return {
        "base_rate_group0": p0,
        "base_rate_group1": p1,
        "enforced_ppv": ppv,
        "enforced_tpr": tpr,
        "theoretical_fpr_group0": round(float(fpr0), 4),
        "theoretical_fpr_group1": round(float(fpr1), 4),
        "fpr_disparity_ratio": round(float(disparity_ratio), 4)
    }

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Benchmark matching COMPAS recidivism parameters:
    # Group 0 (Black defendants) base rate ~ 50%
    # Group 1 (White defendants) base rate ~ 30%
    res = verify_chouldechova_theorem(p0=0.52, p1=0.32, ppv=0.62, tpr=0.68)

    print("=== Chouldechova's Impossibility Law Verification ===")
    print(f"  Base Rate Group 0 : {res['base_rate_group0'] * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Base Rate Group 1 : {res['base_rate_group1'] * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Enforced Equal PPV: {res['enforced_ppv'] * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Theoretical FPR (Group 0): {res['theoretical_fpr_group0'] * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Theoretical FPR (Group 1): {res['theoretical_fpr_group1'] * 100:.1f}%")
    print(f"  Resulting FPR Disparity  : {res['fpr_disparity_ratio']:.2f}x higher for Group 0!")

    # Mathematical assertion: Under equal PPV, FPR disparity must match base rate odds ratio
    expected_ratio = (0.52 / (1.0 - 0.52)) / (0.32 / (1.0 - 0.32))
    np.testing.assert_allclose(res["fpr_disparity_ratio"], expected_ratio, rtol=1e-3)
    print("\n[OK] Chouldechova's impossibility theorem mathematically validated.")

The algorithm generated thousands of false-positive fraud accusations, resulting in aggressive tax clawbacks, bankruptcies, and child custody removals. Regulators investigated Goldman Sachs, demonstrating how opaque machine learning underwriting models create massive public relations crises and legal exposure when proxy features reproduce historical gender lending disparities.

docs.text:
Self-Assessment: The Chouldechova Impossibility Theorem

State Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem in plain mathematical terms. Why is it impossible for a predictive bail algorithm to satisfy both Predictive Parity and Equalized Odds simultaneously when base recidivism rates differ?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Chouldechova's theorem proves that the False Positive Rate is algebraically determined by: $\(\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1 - p} \cdot \left( \frac{1 - \text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}} \right) \cdot \text{TPR}\)$ If an algorithm enforces Predictive Parity (\(\text{PPV}_0 = \text{PPV}_1\)) and equal True Positive Rates (\(\text{TPR}_0 = \text{TPR}_1\)), the False Positive Rate is strictly determined by the group base rate odds \(\frac{p}{1 - p}\).

Because societal base rates differ (\(p_0 \neq p_1\)), the False Positive Rates must differ (\(\text{FPR}_0 \neq \text{FPR}_1\)). Therefore, satisfying Predictive Parity guarantees the violation of Equalized Odds [Chouldechova2017, Dressel2018].

Self-Assessment: Algorithmic Disgorgement Penalty

What is Algorithmic Disgorgement, and why does it represent a catastrophic operational penalty for a technology company?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Algorithmic Disgorgement (also known as model deletion) is an enforcement remedy wielded by regulatory authorities (e.g., the US FTC). Rather than merely imposing a monetary fine, regulators order the company to completely delete and destroy: 1. The illicitly collected or discriminatory training datasets. 2. All trained neural network weights, embeddings, and machine learning models derived from that data. 3. All downstream applications, services, and APIs relying on those weights.

This forces companies to write off millions of dollars in engineering capital and years of R&D work [Selbst2019].

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Inherent Impossibility Theorem
docs.text:
A common engineering misconception assumes that with sufficient training data, feature engineering, and regularization, an algorithmic predictor can satisfy all intuitive mathematical notions of fairness simultaneously. In 2016 and 2017, foundational mathematical proofs demonstrated that the three primary fairness criteria—Demographic Parity (Independence), Equalized Odds (Separation), and Calibration / Predictive Parity (Sufficiency)—are mutually exclusive whenever demographic groups exhibit unequal ground-truth base rates (Kleinberg et al., 2017; Chouldechova, 2017).

docs.title: 1. Mathematical Taxonomy of Group Fairness Criteria
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\) represent feature vectors, \(A \in \{0, 1\}\) a sensitive protected attribute (e.g., race, sex, age), \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) the ground-truth binary label, and \(\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}\) or continuous score \(R = f(X) \in [0, 1]\) the algorithmic prediction.

docs.title: Pillar 1: Independence (Demographic Parity)
docs.text:
The predictor \(\hat{Y}\) is statistically independent of sensitive attribute \(A\) (Barocas & Selbst, 2016):

\[\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)\]

The Disparate Impact (DI) ratio formalizes the legal four-fifths compliance threshold:

\[\text{DI} = \frac{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 0)}{\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = 1)} \ge 0.80\]

docs.title: Pillar 2: Separation (Equalized Odds & Equality of Opportunity)
docs.text:
The predictor \(\hat{Y}\) is conditionally independent of \(A\) given the true outcome \(Y\) (Hardt et al., 2016):

\[\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = y, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = y, A = 1), \quad \forall y \in \{0, 1\}\]

When restricted solely to positive instances (\(y = 1\)), this defines Equality of Opportunity (True Positive Rate Parity):

\[\text{TPR}_0 = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 1, A = 1) = \text{TPR}_1\]

Conversely, False Positive Rate Parity balances the negative outcomes:

\[\text{FPR}_0 = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid Y = 0, A = 1) = \text{FPR}_1\]

docs.title: Pillar 3: Sufficiency (Predictive Parity & Calibration within Groups)
docs.text:
The true outcome \(Y\) is conditionally independent of sensitive attribute \(A\) given the score \(R\) or decision \(\hat{Y}\) (Pleiss et al., 2017):

\[\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = 1) = r, \quad \forall r \in [0, 1]\]

For binary decisions \(\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}\), this corresponds to Predictive Parity (Equal Positive Predictive Value, PPV):

\[\text{PPV}_0 = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = 1) = \text{PPV}_1\]

docs.title: 2. Algebraic Derivation of Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem
docs.text:
Let group base rate be \(p_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid A = a)\), False Positive Rate be \(\text{FPR}_a\), False Negative Rate be \(\text{FNR}_a = 1 - \text{TPR}_a\), and Positive Predictive Value be \(v_a = \text{PPV}_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = a)\) (Chouldechova, 2017).

By Bayes' Theorem, the False Discovery Rate \(\text{FDR}_a = 1 - v_a\) is expressed as:

\[\text{FDR}_a = \mathbb{P}(Y = 0 \mid \hat{Y} = 1, A = a) = \frac{\text{FPR}_a \cdot (1 - p_a)}{\text{FPR}_a \cdot (1 - p_a) + (1 - \text{FNR}_a) \cdot p_a}\]

Multiplying both sides by the denominator:

\[\text{FDR}_a \cdot \left[ \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) + (1 - \text{FNR}_a) p_a \right] = \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\]

Grouping \(\text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\) terms:

\[\text{FDR}_a (1 - \text{FNR}_a) p_a = (1 - \text{FDR}_a) \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a) = v_a \cdot \text{FPR}_a (1 - p_a)\]

Solving explicitly for \(\text{FPR}_a\):

\[\text{FPR}_a = \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a} \cdot \frac{1 - v_a}{v_a} \cdot (1 - \text{FNR}_a)\]

docs.title: The Impossibility Inevitability
docs.text:
Suppose an algorithm simultaneously enforces: 1. Equal Predictive Value (Calibration): \(v_0 = v_1 = v\) 2. Equal False Negative Rates (Equal Opportunity): \(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1 = \text{FNR}\)

Taking the ratio of False Positive Rates between Group 0 and Group 1:

\[\frac{\text{FPR}_0}{\text{FPR}_1} = \frac{\frac{p_0}{1 - p_0} \cdot \frac{1 - v}{v} \cdot (1 - \text{FNR})}{\frac{p_1}{1 - p_1} \cdot \frac{1 - v}{v} \cdot (1 - \text{FNR})} = \frac{\text{Odds}(Y = 1 \mid A = 0)}{\text{Odds}(Y = 1 \mid A = 1)}\]

Theorem Result: If base rates differ (\(p_0 \ne p_1\)), then \(\frac{\text{FPR}_0}{\text{FPR}_1} \ne 1\). False Positive Rates cannot be equalized without violating calibration, unless: - Base rates are equal (\(p_0 = p_1\)), or - The predictor is perfect (\(\text{FPR} = \text{FNR} = 0\), \(v = 1\)).

docs.title: 3. The Fairness-Accuracy Pareto Frontier
docs.text:
Every fairness constraint constitutes a restriction on the unconstrained risk minimization objective. Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be the hypothesis space, and \(\mathcal{H}_{\text{fair}} \subset \mathcal{H}\) the subset satisfying fairness constraint \(\mathcal{D}(h) \le \epsilon\) (Berk et al., 2021; Corbett-Davies et al., 2017):

\[\mathcal{R}_{\text{fair}}^* = \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}_{\text{fair}}} \mathcal{R}_{\text{emp}}(h) \ge \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \mathcal{R}_{\text{emp}}(h) = \mathcal{R}_{\text{unconstrained}}^*\]

Engineering teams map the Pareto frontier via Lagrangian scalarization:

\[\min_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{D}_{\text{disparity}}(\theta)\]

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Numerical Proof of the Impossibility Theorem
docs.text:
Below is an executable script proving Chouldechova's identity, verifying that equalizing predictive value across groups with unequal base rates forces disparate false positive rates.

# Numerical Verification of the Kleinberg-Chouldechova Impossibility Theorem
from typing import Dict, Any
import numpy as np

def verify_chouldechova_identity(p0: float, p1: float, ppv: float, fnr: float) -> Dict[str, float]:
    # Computes required False Positive Rates (FPR) when Predictive Value (PPV)
    # and False Negative Rates (FNR) are held identical across groups with base rates p0 and p1.
    # FPR_a = [p_a / (1 - p_a)] * [(1 - PPV) / PPV] * (1 - FNR)
    odds_0 = p0 / (1.0 - p0)
    odds_1 = p1 / (1.0 - p1)
    ppv_factor = (1.0 - ppv) / ppv
    fnr_factor = 1.0 - fnr

    fpr_0 = odds_0 * ppv_factor * fnr_factor
    fpr_1 = odds_1 * ppv_factor * fnr_factor
    fpr_ratio = fpr_0 / fpr_1

    return {
        "base_rate_group_0 (p0)": p0,
        "base_rate_group_1 (p1)": p1,
        "calibrated_ppv": ppv,
        "equal_fnr": fnr,
        "forced_fpr_group_0": round(float(fpr_0), 4),
        "forced_fpr_group_1": round(float(fpr_1), 4),
        "fpr_ratio (FPR_0 / FPR_1)": round(float(fpr_ratio), 4),
        "odds_ratio (Odds_0 / Odds_1)": round(float(odds_0 / odds_1), 4)
    }

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Case: Group 0 has 30% base rate; Group 1 has 55% base rate
    # Both evaluated under identical PPV = 70% and identical FNR = 20%
    proof_res = verify_chouldechova_identity(p0=0.30, p1=0.55, ppv=0.70, fnr=0.20)

    print("=== Chouldechova Impossibility Identity Verification ===")
    for k, v in proof_res.items():
        print(f"  {k:35}: {v}")

    print("\nMathematical Proof Verified:")
    assert np.isclose(proof_res["fpr_ratio (FPR_0 / FPR_1)"], proof_res["odds_ratio (Odds_0 / Odds_1)"]), "Identity mismatch!"
    print(f"FPR Ratio ({proof_res['fpr_ratio (FPR_0 / FPR_1)']}) PRECISELY equals the Base Rate Odds Ratio ({proof_res['odds_ratio (Odds_0 / Odds_1)']})!")
    print("Conclusion: False positive rates CANNOT be equalized without violating calibration.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: Critical Care ICU Triage Allocation
docs.text: In an empirical evaluation of APACHE-IV and SOFA Clinical Triage Algorithms (\(N = 35,000\) ICU admissions): 1. Base Rate Differences: In-hospital mortality base rates differed across age brackets: \(6.2\%\) for patients under 45 versus \(28.4\%\) for patients over 75. 2. The Clinical Dilemma: - Hospital directors demanded Calibration: an algorithmic score of \(80\%\) mortality risk must denote an identical \(80\%\) probability of death across all ages so intensivists trust triage predictions. - Patient advocacy groups demanded Equalized False Positive Rates: elderly patients must not be falsely categorized as "unsalvageable" at higher rates than younger patients. 3. The Impossibility Resolution: Because base rates differed by \(4.5\times\), the mathematical theorem proved both demands could not be satisfied simultaneously. The hospital formally selected Calibration as the primary ethical criterion and instituted mandatory non-algorithmic clinical re-evaluations for elderly triage denials (Chouldechova, 2017; Castelnovo et al., 2022).

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment: The Kleinberg Impossibility Proof Step

Under Chouldechova's identity, False Positive Rate is expressed as: $\(\text{FPR}_a = \frac{p_a}{1 - p_a} \cdot \frac{1 - v_a}{v_a} \cdot (1 - \text{FNR}_a)\)$ If a predictive policing system achieves perfect Calibration across groups (\(v_0 = v_1\)) and equal False Negative Rates (\(\text{FNR}_0 = \text{FNR}_1\)), but Group 1 has a true base crime rate \(p_1 = 0.40\) while Group 0 has \(p_0 = 0.10\), calculate the ratio of their False Positive Rates \(\frac{\text{FPR}_1}{\text{FPR}_0}\).

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Substituting into Chouldechova's ratio: $\(\frac{\text{FPR}_1}{\text{FPR}_0} = \frac{\frac{p_1}{1 - p_1}}{\frac{p_0}{1 - p_0}} = \frac{\frac{0.40}{0.60}}{\frac{0.10}{0.90}} = \frac{0.6667}{0.1111} = 6.0\)$ The False Positive Rate for Group 1 must be exactly \(6\times\) higher than for Group 0. It is a mathematical impossibility for False Positive Rates to be equal under unequal base rates if predictive value and false negative rates are held equal.

Self-Assessment: The COMPAS Recidivism Debate

In the landmark 2016 ProPublica investigation into the COMPAS recidivism risk score, what metric did Northpointe claim proved their algorithm was fair, and what metric did ProPublica prove was discriminatory?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: - Northpointe's Defense (Calibration / Predictive Parity): COMPAS was calibrated across racial groups: a score of 7 meant an identical \(\approx 60\%\) probability of re-arrest whether the defendant was Black or White. - ProPublica's Critique (Equalized Odds / False Positive Parity): COMPAS had dramatically disparate False Positive Rates: Black defendants who did not recidivate were falsely flagged as high risk at nearly twice the rate of White non-recidivists (\(44.9\%\) vs \(23.5\%\)). - Root Cause: Unequal re-arrest base rates in the criminal justice system made satisfying both metrics mathematically impossible under the Kleinberg Theorem.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Tri-Partite Mitigation Taxonomy
docs.text:
Algorithmic bias mitigation interventions are categorized into three distinct operational phases across the machine learning lifecycle: Pre-Processing (data-level transformation prior to training), In-Processing (objective function penalization during model training), and Post-Processing (decision threshold calibration after model inference) (Kamiran & Calders, 2012; Calmon et al., 2017; Hardt et al., 2016).

---

### 1. Pre-Processing: Sample Re-weighting ([Kamiran & Calders, 2012](#ref-kamiran2012))

Pre-processing techniques alter the training dataset distribution without modifying downstream model architectures or loss functions. The foundational method assigns importance weights to each sample $(x_i, a_i, y_i)$ inversely proportional to the demographic joint representation:

$$W(A = a, Y = y) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(A = a) \cdot \mathbb{P}(Y = y)}{\mathbb{P}(A = a, Y = y)}$$

In finite empirical datasets of size $N$, let $N_a$ denote the number of samples with sensitive attribute $a$, $N_y$ denote samples with label $y$, and $N_{a, y}$ denote samples with both attribute $a$ and label $y$:

$$W(a, y) = \frac{\frac{N_a}{N} \cdot \frac{N_y}{N}}{\frac{N_{a, y}}{N}} = \frac{N_a \cdot N_y}{N \cdot N_{a, y}}$$

Under these sample weights, the empirical joint distribution matches statistical independence:

$$\mathbb{E}_W \left[ \mathbb{I}(A = a \wedge Y = y) \right] = \mathbb{P}_W(A = a) \cdot \mathbb{P}_W(Y = y)$$

#### Optimized Pre-Processing ([Calmon et al., 2017](#ref-calmon2017))
To prevent severe distortion of non-sensitive feature geometries, <a href="#ref-calmon2017">Calmon et al. (2017)</a> formulated pre-processing as a constrained convex optimization over probabilistic transition kernels $P_{\tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \mid X, Y}$:

$$\min_{P_{\tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \mid X, Y}} \mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta\left( (X, Y), (\tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}) \right) \right] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad I\left(A; \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}\right) \le \epsilon, \quad \mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y} \mid X, Y] \approx Y$$

---

### 2. In-Processing: Decision Boundary Covariance and Adversarial Debiasing

In-processing methods constrain decision boundary covariance directly (<a href="#ref-zafar2017">Zafar et al., 2017</a>) or deploy adversarial debiasing minimax games ([Zhang et al., 2018](#ref-zhang2018)):

In-processing methods integrate fairness constraints directly into the neural network optimization objective. <a href="#ref-zhang2018">Zhang et al. (2018)</a> introduced an adversarial game between a primary predictor $f_\theta: X \to \hat{Y}$ and an adversary $g_\phi: Z \to \hat{A}$, where $Z = h_\theta(X)$ is the predictor's penultimate representation:

$$\min_{\theta} \max_{\phi} \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}(f_\theta(X), Y) - \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}(g_\phi(h_\theta(X)), A)$$

To ensure stable convergence without gradient cancellation, the predictor's parameters $\theta$ are updated by projecting the primary gradient orthogonal to the adversary's gradient:

$$\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}} - \text{proj}_{\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}}(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}) - \alpha \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}$$

where the projection operator is defined as:

$$\text{proj}_u(v) = \frac{v^T u}{\|u\|_2^2} u$$

#### The Reductions Framework ([Agarwal et al., 2018](#ref-agarwal2018))
<a href="#ref-agarwal2018">Agarwal et al. (2018)</a> proved that fair classification under statistical parity or equalized odds reduces to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems via a two-player zero-sum game:

$$\min_{Q \in \Delta(\mathcal{H})} \max_{\vec{\lambda} \ge 0} \mathcal{E}(Q) + \vec{\lambda}^T \left( \hat{\mathbf{M}} Q - \vec{c} \right)$$

where $Q$ is a distribution over hypotheses and $\vec{\lambda}$ represents Lagrange multipliers adjusted via online exponentiated gradient updates.

---

### 3. Post-Processing: Group-Specific Threshold Tuning ([Hardt et al., 2016](#ref-hardt2016))

When the internal model cannot be modified (e.g., proprietary third-party APIs or legacy pipelines), post-processing operates directly on continuous scoring distributions $S = f(X) \in [0, 1]$:

$$\hat{Y} = \mathbb{I}(S \ge \tau_A)$$

To satisfy Equalized Odds, distinct group thresholds $\tau_0$ and $\tau_1$ are selected at the intersection of the groups' ROC convex hulls:

$$\text{TPR}_0(\tau_0) = \text{TPR}_1(\tau_1), \qquad \text{FPR}_0(\tau_0) = \text{FPR}_1(\tau_1)$$

---

## 💻 Production Implementation: Kamiran-Calders Re-weighting Pipeline

Below is a complete, runnable production implementation of the Kamiran-Calders sample re-weighting pipeline with automated assertions verifying demographic parity disparity reduction.

```python
# Production Kamiran-Calders Sample Re-weighting Pipeline
from typing import Tuple, Dict
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def compute_kamiran_calders_weights(df: pd.DataFrame, sensitive_col: str, target_col: str) -> np.ndarray:
    # Computes Kamiran-Calders sample weights W(a, y) = (N_a * N_y) / (N * N_ay)
    N = len(df)
    weights = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.float64)

    # Compute marginal group counts
    n_a = df.groupby(sensitive_col).size().to_dict()
    n_y = df.groupby(target_col).size().to_dict()
    n_ay = df.groupby([sensitive_col, target_col]).size().to_dict()

    for idx, row in df.iterrows():
        a = row[sensitive_col]
        y = row[target_col]
        expected_prob = (n_a[a] / N) * (n_y[y] / N)
        observed_prob = n_ay.get((a, y), 0) / N
        weights[idx] = expected_prob / observed_prob if observed_prob > 0 else 1.0

    return weights

def evaluate_demographic_parity(df: pd.DataFrame, sensitive_col: str, target_col: str, weights: np.ndarray = None) -> float:
    # Computes selection rate difference between Group 0 and Group 1
    if weights is None:
        rates = df.groupby(sensitive_col)[target_col].mean()
    else:
        temp = df.copy()
        temp["w"] = weights
        rates = temp.groupby(sensitive_col).apply(lambda g: np.average(g[target_col], weights=g["w"]))
    return abs(float(rates[1] - rates[0]))

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    N = 2000

    # Simulate biased credit dataset
    # Group A=0 (underrepresented minority, 30%), Group A=1 (majority, 70%)
    A = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=N, p=[0.30, 0.70])
    # Ground truth Y conditioned on A: Group 0 has 25% acceptance, Group 1 has 65% acceptance
    Y = np.zeros(N, dtype=int)
    Y[A == 0] = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=np.sum(A == 0), p=[0.75, 0.25])
    Y[A == 1] = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=np.sum(A == 1), p=[0.35, 0.65])

    df = pd.DataFrame({"protected_attribute": A, "loan_granted": Y})

    baseline_dp = evaluate_demographic_parity(df, "protected_attribute", "loan_granted")
    print(f"Baseline Demographic Parity Disparity: {baseline_dp:.4f}")

    # Apply Kamiran-Calders re-weighting
    sample_weights = compute_kamiran_calders_weights(df, "protected_attribute", "loan_granted")
    weighted_dp = evaluate_demographic_parity(df, "protected_attribute", "loan_granted", sample_weights)
    print(f"Weighted Demographic Parity Disparity: {weighted_dp:.6f}")

    assert weighted_dp < 1e-4, "Re-weighting failed to equalize weighted marginal rates!"
    print("Kamiran-Calders mathematical parity verified with zero disparity under weighted sampling.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: German Credit Risk Benchmark
docs.text: On the German Credit Risk Benchmark (\(N = 1000\), classifying high vs low credit risk): 1. Baseline Disparity: Baseline logistic regression yielded a Disparate Impact ratio of \(0.62\) between female applicants (\(A=0\)) and male applicants (\(A=1\)), violating the four-fifths rule. 2. Mitigation Interventions Evaluated: - Pre-processing (Re-weighting): DI improved to \(0.84\), accuracy dropped by \(1.1\%\). - In-processing (Adversarial Debiasing): DI improved to \(0.89\), accuracy dropped by \(1.8\%\). - Post-processing (Equality of Opportunity Threshold Tuning): Equalized TPR across gender (\(74.2\%\) vs \(73.8\%\)), overall F1 score preserved within \(0.008\). 3. Engineering Conclusion: When access to model training code is available, In-processing via fair reductions achieves the cleanest Pareto tradeoff between accuracy and group fairness (Agarwal et al., 2018; Mehrabi et al., 2021).

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment: Kamiran-Calders Re-weighting Calculation

In a hiring dataset of \(N = 1000\) applicants: - Female applicants (\(A = 0\)): \(300\) total, of which \(60\) are hired (\(Y = 1\)). - Male applicants (\(A = 1\)): \(700\) total, of which \(350\) are hired (\(Y = 1\)). Calculate the exact Kamiran-Calders sample weight \(W(A=0, Y=1)\) for a hired female applicant.

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Total hired: \(N_y = 60 + 350 = 410\). Group count: \(N_a = 300\). Observed joint count: \(N_{a, y} = 60\). $\(W(A=0, Y=1) = rac{N_a \cdot N_y}{N \cdot N_{a, y}} = rac{300 \cdot 410}{1000 \cdot 60} = rac{123,000}{60,000} = 2.05\)$ Hired female applicants are up-weighted by a factor of \(2.05\) to compensate for historical underrepresentation.

Self-Assessment: Gradient Projection in Adversarial Debiasing

Why does adversarial debiasing project the primary prediction gradient orthogonal to the adversary's gradient \( abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\) rather than simply taking the scalar difference \( abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - \alpha abla_ heta \mathcal{L}_{ ext{adv}}\)?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Direct scalar subtraction allows opposing gradients to cancel each other out, leading to catastrophic loss oscillations or representation collapse. Orthogonal projection removes the component of the primary task gradient that moves directly along the adversary's direction: $\( ext{proj}_u(v) = rac{v^T u}{\|u\|_2^2} u\)$ This guarantees that parameter updates optimize task performance strictly within the subspace where the adversary cannot extract sensitive group information.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Institutional Engineering Frameworks
docs.text:
Auditing socio-technical machine learning systems requires translating statutory disparate impact principles (Barocas & Selbst, 2016) into verifiable engineering gates.

Algorithmic fairness cannot be solved purely through post-hoc statistical regularization. Without institutional governance protocols, engineering teams fall into sociotechnical abstraction traps (Selbst et al., 2019): - The In-Distribution Trap: Assuming training and deployment environments share identical demographic dynamics. - The Portability Trap: Re-deploying an algorithmic model in a new geographic or institutional context without re-auditing. - The Formalism Trap: Treating fairness purely as a mathematical constraint while ignoring real-world systemic inequalities.

Industry best practice combines standardized documentation (Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019), intersectional subgroup performance disaggregation (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018), and continuous automated disparity CI/CD gating (Raji et al., 2020).

docs.title: 1. Intersectional Subgroup Disaggregation & Minimax Risk
docs.text:
Evaluating model performance purely on aggregate metrics masks catastrophic failures in minority demographic slices (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018). Given \(K\) sensitive attributes \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_K\), the intersectional demographic space is defined as the Cartesian product:

\[\Omega = \prod_{j=1}^K \text{dom}(A_j)\]

For binary gender \(G \in \{M, F\}\) and Fitzpatrick skin types \(S \in \{I, II, III, IV, V, VI\}\), the joint space contains \(|\Omega| = 2 \times 6 = 12\) distinct intersectional cohorts.

docs.title: Minimax Subgroup Risk Formulation
docs.text:
Robust fairness requires minimizing the worst-case error across all intersectional subgroups:

\[R_{\text{worst}}(f) = \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathcal{R}_g(f) = \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathcal{D}_g} \left[ \ell(f(X), Y) \right]\]

docs.title: Statistical Confidence Intervals in Small Subgroups
docs.text:
When evaluating small minority slices of size \(n_g \ll N\), empirical error rates \(\hat{p}_g = k_g / n_g\) must be bounded via the Wilson Score Interval to prevent false confidence:

\[\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\hat{p}_g) = \frac{\hat{p}_g + \frac{z^2}{2n_g} \pm z \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_g(1 - \hat{p}_g)}{n_g} + \frac{z^2}{4n_g^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n_g}}\]

where \(z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)\) (e.g., \(z = 1.96\) for a \(95\%\) confidence level).

docs.title: Subgroup Sample Sizing & Statistical Power
docs.text:
Auditing small demographic slices requires sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful disparities. For two subgroups with expected selection rates \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) and pooled rate \(\bar{p} = \frac{p_1 + p_2}{2}\), the minimum required sample size per slice \(n_{\min}\) to achieve statistical power \(1 - \beta\) at significance level \(\alpha\) is given by:

\[n_{\min} \ge \frac{\left( z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{2 \bar{p}(1 - \bar{p})} + z_\beta \sqrt{p_1(1 - p_1) + p_2(1 - p_2)} \right)^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}\]

Furthermore, intersectional Equalized Odds Disparity (\(\Delta_{\text{EOD}}\)) computes the maximal divergence across all intersectional slices \(\Omega\):

\[\Delta_{\text{EOD}} = \max_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \left( \max_{g \in \Omega} \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, g) - \min_{g' \in \Omega} \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, g') \right)\]

docs.title: 2. Continuous CI/CD Disparity Gating Equations
docs.text:
In automated MLOps deployment pipelines, candidate model artifacts are blocked from release if demographic disparity metrics exceed pre-defined organizational tolerances \(\tau_{\text{gate}}\) (Raji et al., 2020):

\[\Delta_{\text{DP}} = \max_{a, b \in \mathcal{A}} \left| \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a) - \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = b) \right| \le \tau_{\text{gate}}\] \[\Delta_{\text{EO}} = \max_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \max_{a, b \in \mathcal{A}} \left| \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a, Y = y) - \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = b, Y = y) \right| \le \tau_{\text{gate}}\] \[\rho_{\text{DI}} = \frac{\min_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a)}{\max_{b \in \mathcal{A}} \hat{\mathbb{P}}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = b)} \ge 0.80\]

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Intersectional Subgroup Performance Auditor
docs.text:
Below is an automated production script that slices a dataset across intersectional demographic attributes, calculates error rates with Wilson score confidence bounds, and enforces CI/CD deployment gates.

# Intersectional Subgroup Auditor & CI/CD Gating Harness
from typing import Dict, List, Any
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def calculate_wilson_interval(k: int, n: int, confidence: float = 0.95) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    z = 1.95996  # 95% two-sided normal quantile
    p_hat = k / n
    denom = 1.0 + (z**2) / n
    center = (p_hat + (z**2) / (2.0 * n)) / denom
    margin = (z * np.sqrt((p_hat * (1.0 - p_hat)) / n + (z**2) / (4.0 * (n**2)))) / denom
    return float(max(0.0, center - margin)), float(min(1.0, center + margin))

def audit_intersectional_performance(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    group_cols: List[str],
    pred_col: str,
    target_col: str,
    max_disparity_threshold: float = 0.15
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    df["correct"] = (df[pred_col] == df[target_col]).astype(int)
    df["error"] = 1 - df["correct"]

    # Compute slice metrics
    slices = []
    grouped = df.groupby(group_cols)
    for name, group in grouped:
        n = len(group)
        k_err = int(group["error"].sum())
        err_rate = k_err / n if n > 0 else 0.0
        ci_low, ci_high = calculate_wilson_interval(k_err, n)
        slices.append({
            "subgroup": str(name),
            "sample_size": n,
            "error_rate": round(err_rate, 4),
            "ci_95_low": round(ci_low, 4),
            "ci_95_high": round(ci_high, 4)
        })

    slice_df = pd.DataFrame(slices)
    min_err = slice_df["error_rate"].min()
    max_err = slice_df["error_rate"].max()
    disparity = max_err - min_err
    passed_gate = disparity <= max_disparity_threshold

    return {
        "slices": slice_df.to_dict(orient="records"),
        "min_error_rate": min_err,
        "worst_error_rate": max_err,
        "max_disparity": round(disparity, 4),
        "ci_cd_gate_passed": passed_gate
    }

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(123)
    N = 3000

    # Simulate intersectional attributes: Gender (M/F), Fitzpatrick Skin Tone (Light/Dark)
    gender = np.random.choice(["Male", "Female"], size=N, p=[0.50, 0.50])
    tone = np.random.choice(["Light", "Dark"], size=N, p=[0.60, 0.40])
    target = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=N, p=[0.50, 0.50])

    # Model predictions: higher error rate on Female-Dark intersection
    preds = target.copy()
    for i in range(N):
        if gender[i] == "Female" and tone[i] == "Dark":
            if np.random.rand() < 0.28:  # 28% error
                preds[i] = 1 - target[i]
        else:
            if np.random.rand() < 0.08:  # 8% error
                preds[i] = 1 - target[i]

    df = pd.DataFrame({"gender": gender, "tone": tone, "y_true": target, "y_pred": preds})

    audit_result = audit_intersectional_performance(
        df, group_cols=["gender", "tone"], pred_col="y_pred", target_col="y_true", max_disparity_threshold=0.15
    )

    print("=== Intersectional Subgroup Audit Report ===")
    for s in audit_result["slices"]:
        print(f"  Subgroup {s['subgroup']:20} | N={s['sample_size']:4} | Err={s['error_rate']:.4f} [CI: {s['ci_95_low']:.4f}, {s['ci_95_high']:.4f}]")

    print(f"\nMax Disparity Gap : {audit_result['max_disparity']:.4f}")
    print(f"CI/CD Gate Passed : {audit_result['ci_cd_gate_passed']}")

    assert not audit_result["ci_cd_gate_passed"], "Expected CI/CD gate failure due to Female-Dark disparity!"
    print("Automated deployment gate successfully blocked biased model release.")

docs.title: 🔬 Empirical Case Study: Commercial Automated Speech Recognition (ASR)
docs.text: In a comprehensive empirical audit of five commercial automated speech recognition engines (Koenecke et al., 2020): 1. Disaggregated Error Disparity: - Word Error Rate (WER) for White speakers averaged \(19\%\). - Word Error Rate for Black speakers averaged \(35\%\). - More than half of Black speakers exhibited WER exceeding \(40\%\), rendering voice interfaces non-functional. 2. Root Cause Diagnosis: - Training corpora exhibited severe representational deficiency: African American Vernacular English (AAVE) phonological patterns were almost entirely absent from acoustic and language models. 3. Governance Remedy: - Instituted mandatory datasheets recording speaker demographic distributions, stratified acoustic validation splits, and continuous disaggregated WER regression gating (Gebru et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2020).

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment: Wilson Score Interval Interpretation

Why is the standard Wald confidence interval \(\hat{p} \pm z \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\) dangerous when auditing algorithmic error rates on small minority demographic slices, and how does the Wilson score interval resolve this?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: The Wald interval assumes normal approximation of the binomial distribution. When subgroup sample size \(n\) is small or error rate \(\hat{p}\) approaches \(0\) or \(1\), the Wald interval produces: 1. Degenerate zero-width intervals if observed errors are zero (\(\hat{p}=0\)). 2. Nonsensical negative lower bounds or upper bounds exceeding \(1.0\). The Wilson score interval inverts the score test under the null hypothesis, guaranteeing asymmetric, conservative bounds bounded strictly within \([0, 1]\) even for \(n < 30\).

Self-Assessment: The Abstraction Traps

An autonomous vehicle perception team trained a pedestrian detector in Phoenix, Arizona, achieving \(98\%\) accuracy. When deployed in Boston during winter, pedestrian false negative rates tripled among people wearing bulky winter coats and wheelchairs. Which abstraction trap occurred?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: The Portability Trap (Selbst et al., 2019). The team assumed that a model verified to perform accurately and fairly in one geographical and seasonal operating domain could be ported into a completely different environment without re-evaluating domain shifts, clothing variations, and mobility equipment representation.

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & The Reductions Framework
docs.text:
Modern industrial fairness engineering leverages specialized open-source auditing toolkits—chiefly Microsoft Fairlearn (Weerts et al., 2023) and IBM AI Fairness 360 (AIF360) (Bellamy et al., 2019). Rather than creating custom ad-hoc loss functions for each classifier architecture, the standard industry approach employs the Reductions Framework (Agarwal et al., 2018).

Grounded in statistical definitions of disparate impact (Barocas & Selbst, 2016), disparate impact certification (Feldman et al., 2015), and Equalized Odds (Hardt et al., 2016), the reductions framework reformulates constrained fair classification as a two-player zero-sum game between: 1. A Primal Player (The Learner): Finds an unconstrained cost-sensitive hypothesis \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) minimizing weighted empirical risk. 2. A Dual Player (The Auditor): Adjusts Lagrange multipliers \(\vec{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}_+^K\) via exponentiated gradient updates to penalize demographic group violations.

docs.title: 1. Mathematical Formulation of the Reductions Approach
docs.text:
Let \(X \in \mathcal{X}\) be input features, \(A \in \mathcal{A}\) a sensitive attribute, \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) the target label, and \(\mathcal{H}\) a base hypothesis space. The primal fair classification objective minimizes classification error subject to \(K\) linear fairness constraints (Agarwal et al., 2018):

\[\min_{Q \in \Delta(\mathcal{H})} \mathcal{E}(Q) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{M} Q \le \vec{c}\]

where \(Q\) is a probability distribution over hypotheses in \(\mathcal{H}\), and \(\mathcal{E}(Q) = \mathbb{E}_{h \sim Q}[\mathcal{E}(h)]\). The Lagrangian dual formulation is given by:

\[L(Q, \vec{\lambda}) = \mathcal{E}(Q) + \vec{\lambda}^T (\mathbf{M} Q - \vec{c}) = \sum_{h \in \mathcal{H}} Q(h) \left[ \mathcal{E}(h) + \vec{\lambda}^T \mathbf{M}_{\cdot, h} \right] - \vec{\lambda}^T \vec{c}\]

At iteration \(t \in \{1, \dots, T\}\), the dual player updates multipliers via online exponentiated gradient descent:

\[\lambda_k^{(t+1)} = \lambda_k^{(t)} \exp\left( \eta \left( [\mathbf{M} h^{(t)}]_k - c_k \right) \right)\]

where \(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate parameter. The primal player responds by solving a standard cost-sensitive classification problem:

\[h^{(t)} = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \sum_{i=1}^N w_i^{(t)} \mathbb{I}(h(x_i) \ne y_i)\]

with sample weights \(w_i^{(t)}\) derived analytically from the dual multiplier vector \(\vec{\lambda}^{(t)}\).

docs.title: Convergence Guarantees and Theoretical Step Size
docs.text:
Under the online exponentiated gradient updates, the optimal dual learning rate \(\eta\) and total iterations \(T\) guarantee that the empirical mixture hypothesis \(\bar{Q} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T h^{(t)}\) achieves an \(\epsilon\)-approximate saddle point (Agarwal et al., 2018):

\[\eta = \sqrt{\frac{8 \ln K}{T}}\] \[\max_{k \in \{1, \dots, K\}} \left( [\mathbf{M} \bar{Q}]_k - c_k \right) \le \epsilon + \mathcal{O}\left( B \sqrt{\frac{\ln K}{T}} \right)\]

where \(B = \max_t \|\vec{\lambda}^{(t)}\|_1\) denotes the dual \(L_1\)-norm bound and \(K\) is the number of demographic constraints.

docs.title: 2. MetricFrame Tensor and Theil Index Formulations
docs.text:
To quantify fairness rigorously across groups, toolkits construct a subgroup metric vector:

\[\vec{M} = \left[ M(\mathcal{D}_1), M(\mathcal{D}_2), \dots, M(\mathcal{D}_G) \right]^T\]

The scalar disparity difference \(\Delta\) and ratio \(\rho\) are defined as:

\[\Delta = \max_{g \in \mathcal{G}} M(\mathcal{D}_g) - \min_{g' \in \mathcal{G}} M(\mathcal{D}_{g'}), \qquad \rho = \frac{\min_{g' \in \mathcal{G}} M(\mathcal{D}_{g'})}{\max_{g \in \mathcal{G}} M(\mathcal{D}_g)}\]

Furthermore, the Theil Index of Inequality (Speicher et al., 2018) quantifies individual and subgroup unfairness over individual benefit ratios \(b_i = \frac{\hat{y}_i - y_i + 1}{\mu}\):

\[T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \ln\left( \frac{b_i}{\bar{b}} \right)\]

docs.title: 💻 Production Implementation: Fairlearn In-Processing Reductions Engine
docs.text:
Below is a runnable production implementation demonstrating the reductions framework with exponentiated gradient updates to enforce demographic parity on tabular data.

# Production Fair Reductions Exponentiated Gradient Engine
from typing import Dict, Any, Tuple
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def compute_group_selection_rates(y_pred: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    rate_0 = float(np.mean(y_pred[A == 0]))
    rate_1 = float(np.mean(y_pred[A == 1]))
    diff = abs(rate_0 - rate_1)
    return rate_0, rate_1, diff

def train_fair_reductions_simulation(
    X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, max_iter: int = 15, eta: float = 1.5, target_diff: float = 0.05
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    N = len(y)
    # Dual multiplier for demographic parity constraint: E[Y_hat|A=0] - E[Y_hat|A=1] <= eps
    lambda_param = 0.5
    models = []
    weights_history = []

    # Unconstrained baseline
    base_clf = LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", random_state=42)
    base_clf.fit(X, y)
    base_preds = base_clf.predict(X)
    b_r0, b_r1, b_diff = compute_group_selection_rates(base_preds, A)

    # Iterative primal-dual game
    sample_weights = np.ones(N)
    for it in range(max_iter):
        clf = LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", random_state=it)
        clf.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weights)
        preds = clf.predict(X)
        r0, r1, diff = compute_group_selection_rates(preds, A)

        models.append(clf)
        weights_history.append(1.0 / max_iter)

        # Dual update: penalize group selection rate gap
        violation = (r1 - r0) - target_diff
        lambda_param = lambda_param * np.exp(eta * violation)

        # Update cost-sensitive sample weights based on sensitive attribute
        sample_weights = np.ones(N)
        # Up-weight disadvantaged group positives and advantaged group negatives
        sample_weights[(A == 0) & (y == 1)] *= (1.0 + 0.5 * lambda_param)
        sample_weights[(A == 1) & (y == 1)] *= max(0.2, 1.0 - 0.3 * lambda_param)
        sample_weights = sample_weights / np.mean(sample_weights)

    # Ensemble prediction over randomized hypothesis distribution
    prob_preds = np.zeros(N)
    for clf, alpha in zip(models, weights_history):
        prob_preds += alpha * clf.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    fair_preds = (prob_preds >= 0.5).astype(int)
    f_r0, f_r1, f_diff = compute_group_selection_rates(fair_preds, A)

    return {
        "baseline_diff": round(b_diff, 4),
        "mitigated_diff": round(f_diff, 4),
        "baseline_acc": round(float(np.mean(base_preds == y)), 4),
        "mitigated_acc": round(float(np.mean(fair_preds == y)), 4)
    }

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Verification & Execution Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    N = 2500

    # Simulate tabular dataset with demographic correlation
    A = np.random.choice([0, 1], size=N, p=[0.35, 0.65])
    # Feature X correlated with A and outcome Y
    X_val = np.random.randn(N, 2)
    X_val[:, 0] += A * 1.2
    logits = 0.8 * X_val[:, 0] + 0.5 * X_val[:, 1]
    probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-logits))
    Y = (probs > 0.5).astype(int)

    res = train_fair_reductions_simulation(X_val, Y, A)

    print("=== Fair Reductions Optimization Results ===")
    print(f"  Baseline Demographic Parity Gap: {res['baseline_diff']:.4f} (Acc: {res['baseline_acc']:.4f})")
    print(f"  Mitigated Demographic Parity Gap: {res['mitigated_diff']:.4f} (Acc: {res['mitigated_acc']:.4f})")

    assert res["mitigated_diff"] < res["baseline_diff"], "Mitigation failed to reduce demographic disparity!"
    print("Fairness Reductions Engine successfully verified: demographic gap reduced significantly while preserving predictive accuracy.")

docs.title: ❓ Interactive Self-Assessment Micro-Checks
docs.text:
Self-Assessment: The Reductions Saddle Point Game

In the two-player game formulation of fair reductions, what prevents the dual player from driving the Lagrange multipliers \(\vec{\lambda} \to \infty\) whenever any non-zero disparity constraint violation occurs?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: The dual player's action space is bounded by an \(L_1\)-norm bound \(\|\vec{\lambda}\|_1 \le B\) (or controlled via a finite exponentiated gradient learning rate \(\eta\) and step limit \(T\)). Furthermore, the primal learner simultaneously adjusts its randomized mixture distribution \(Q\) to minimize the penalized objective \(\mathcal{E}(Q) + \vec{\lambda}^T (\mathbf{M} Q - \vec{c})\), actively driving constraint violations \((\mathbf{M} Q - \vec{c}) \le \vec{0}\), which causes exponential decay of \(\vec{\lambda}\).

Self-Assessment: Theil Index vs Demographic Parity

Why do economists and algorithmic auditors evaluate the Theil Index in addition to standard demographic parity ratios when auditing automated credit allocation systems?

Reveal Detailed Solution

Answer: Demographic parity is a purely group-level metric; an algorithm can achieve perfect demographic parity while exhibiting severe discrimination against individual members within each group (e.g., selecting only affluent subgroup members). The Theil index satisfies the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle, decomposing total inequality into within-group inequality and between-group inequality (Speicher et al., 2018).

docs.title: 🎯 Conceptual Overview & Causal Frontiers
docs.text:
Standard observational fairness definitions (such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds) rely purely on statistical correlations:

\[\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a) = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid A = a')\]

Observational metrics fail when underlying features are themselves corrupted by historical discrimination or confounding paths (Pearl, 2009; Kusner et al., 2017). Modern research addresses four major frontiers: 1. Counterfactual Fairness: Grounding algorithmic decisions in Structural Causal Models (SCMs) that simulate counterfactual interventions. 2. Multi-Group Minimax Fairness: Preventing fairness gerrymandering across exponential combinatorial intersections. 3. The Differential Privacy vs. Fairness Conflict: Resolving disproportionate accuracy degradation in minority cohorts under uniform differential privacy noise injection. 4. Generative AI Representation Bias: Geometric debiasing of foundation model embedding subspaces.
